content: Tinea manuum is a fungal infection of the hand caused by dermatophytes, which are a group of fungi that infect keratinized tissues such as the skin, hair, and nails. This condition is classified as a type of dermatophytosis, also known as tinea. It is generally more aggressive than tinea pedis (athlete's foot), although it may appear similar in presentation. Patients with tinea manuum often experience symptoms such as itching, burning, cracking, and scaling of the skin on the hands. The infection can be transmitted through direct contact, including sexual contact, or indirectly via contaminated surfaces, even in the absence of visible symptoms. Diagnosis The diagnosis of tinea manuum is primarily clinical and involves a thorough physical examination of the affected skin. The characteristic findings include scaling, erythema, and sometimes vesicles or pustules on the hands. The diagnosis can be confirmed by microscopic examination of skin scrapings treated with potassium hydroxide (KOH) to identify fungal elements or by fungal culture. Differential Diagnosis Tinea manuum must be distinguished from other dermatological conditions that can present with similar symptoms, such as secondary syphilis, eczema, and pityriasis rosea. These conditions may also cause rashes or scaling, but they have distinct clinical and histopathological features that help differentiate them from tinea manuum. Treatment The treatment of tinea manuum typically involves the use of topical antifungal agents. Selenium sulfide shampoo, applied to the affected area, is one option. In cases where the infection is extensive or does not respond to topical therapy, oral antifungal medications such as griseofulvin may be required.
